paper_title: Specter: Fast MoE Inference via Quantization-Enabled Multi-Step Speculative Offloading

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models often exceed a single accelerator's memory capacity. Offloading experts to host memory creates a severe PCIe I/O bottleneck because data-dependent routing keeps transfers on the critical path. We present Specter, an inference system that uses quantization to combine speculative decoding with expert offloading. Its lightweight quantized draft model runs efficiently on device while preserving high-fidelity expert activation patterns. This provides accurate multi-step lookahead over future expert usage, allowing the runtime to organize expert movement and execution ahead of verification and improve both communication and execution efficiency. Under single-request inference, Specter achieves an average 1.50x (up to 1.88x) speedup in time per output token (TPOT) over the state-of-the-art system. Specter makes memory-constrained, single-GPU MoE inference more practical on commodity hardware. Our code is available at https://github.com/wwwwwf/specter_asplos.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: The mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture [43] has become the de facto standard for scaling large language models Chao Li and Xiaofeng Hou are the corresponding authors. Figure 1. Conventional offloading versus Specter. Aligned quantized speculative decoding lays the foundation for accurate prefetching and efficient system design. (LLMs). By sparsely routing every token to different parameter subsets, MoE models such as Mixtral-8x7B [22], PhiMoE [1], Qwen-MoE [60], and DeepSeek [18] can achieve superior quality without any increase in computational cost. However, its enormous memory footprint presents fundamental deployment challenge, often exceeding the capacity of single accelerator. Offloading inactive experts to host memory [4, 14, 44] is pragmatic solution, which shifts the system bottleneck from computation to data movement. Understanding end-to-end execution bottlenecks on GPUs is crucial for optimizing modern neural networks [19, 58]. In this regard, GPU execution is frequently stalled by PCIe transfers, severely inflating end-to-end inference latency. natural response to mitigate this PCIe latency is expert prefetching [45, 49, 65]. However, the effectiveness of prefetching in MoE inference is fundamentally limited by the autoregressive nature of generation. Because routing decisions are highly input-dependent and strictly sequential, existing prefetching methods are largely restricted to intratoken prediction, i.e., leveraging hidden states from early layers to predict later-layer routes for the current token. This approach only yields microsecond-level computation window, which is fundamentally insufficient to overlap with the millisecond-level PCIe transfer latency of gigabyte-sized experts. Consequently, the GPU remains starved, and significant stalls remain unresolved. To truly hide I/O latency, the system requires multi-step, inter-token lookahead. This observation motivates our key insight: speculative decoding (SD) naturally provides the multi-step lookahead required for aggressive I/O scheduling (Figure 1). Traditionally, SD employs lightweight, independent draft model to rapidly generate future tokens. However, directly applying this paradigm to MoE offloading reveals critical mismatch: standard tiny dense draft model, while extremely memory-efficient, lacks the routing mechanism entirely, making it incapable of predicting which experts the target MoE will activate. Conversely, training smaller independent MoE draft model incurs significant cost and often suffers from routing misalignment with the target model. To resolve this dilemma, we discover that low-bit quantized version (e.g., 4-bit integer (INT4)) of the target MoE model itself serves as an ideal, zero-training-cost predictor. By sharing the identical routing architecture and parameter lineage, this quantized draft guarantees high-fidelity expert activation predictions. As illustrated in Figure 1, Specter leverages this quantized draft to create sufficiently large multi-step time window, orchestrating heavy PCIe transfers well in advance and effectively hiding the I/O latency behind useful computation. Meanwhile, the rigorous draft-then-verify mechanism mathematically guarantees zero degradation in generation quality and output distribution. Turning this intuition into high-performance system, however, exposes severe system-level challenges. Applying SD to MoE models triggers an "expert explosion". In dense models, the verification cost of SD scales gracefully, growing only marginally as the speculation depth 𝐾 increases. In contrast, predicting 𝐾 future tokens in an MoE model simultaneously activates highly diverse set of experts. This sudden burst of demand instantly saturates PCIe bandwidth and overwhelms limited GPU memory. Furthermore, the system must carefully orchestrate asynchronous pipelinesdraft generation, expert prefetching, and target verificationwithout introducing synchronization bubbles. naive integration of SD and MoE offloading simply replaces computation stalls with severe I/O thrashing. While recent works have begun exploring SD for MoE inference, they largely introduce explicit quality-latency tradeoffs [34, 64], or require structurally compatible drafttarget model pairs [7], leaving scheduling and memory wall challenges unresolved. To overcome these challenges, we design and build Specter, co-designed MoE inference acceleration system. We target memory-constrained MoE inference on single GPU, with Wenfeng Wang et al. model weights partially offloaded to host memory. Specter uniquely leverages SD to deliver dual-acceleration paradigm: it utilizes the draft models multi-step lookahead to aggressively prefetch experts and hide millisecond-level PCIe I/O latency, while simultaneously exploiting SDs parallel verification to accelerate the compute-bound generation phase. In summary, Specter consists of the following three core components: Speculative Inference Controller (SIC): We propose novel MoE offloading framework that integrates quantized draft model to provide high-fidelity, multi-step lookahead. The system selects the speculation depth through offline profiling to balance I/O overhead and compute acceleration. Predictive I/O Orchestrator (PIO): To resolve the "expert explosion" bottleneck, we design Prefetch Planner guided by an Expert Lookahead Buffer (ELB). It translates draft predictions into precise, asynchronous PCIe prefetching and cache management, effectively hiding I/O latency behind computation. Streamlined Execution Engine (SEE): We develop highly optimized execution backend that accelerates both phases of SD. It features fused quantized MoE kernels for rapid draft generation and expert-centric computation reordering to streamline target-side verification, eliminating pipeline synchronization bubbles. We implement Specter and evaluate it across three representative MoE architectures under strict hardware constraints. Compared with SpecMoEOff [52], our primary MoE speculative-offloading baseline, Specter achieves an average 1.50 TPOT speedup and up to 1.88 under single-request inference.

sections.title:
2 Background and Motivation
2.1 MoE Offloading Demands Multi-step Lookahead
sections.content: Recently, MoE models have been shown to scale model capacity without increasing computational cost, thus providing higher accuracy [2, 22, 43]. An MoE layer replaces the standard dense feed-forward network (FFN) with set of 𝑁 "expert" networks and trainable router. For each input token, the router dynamically selects small subset of experts (e.g., top-2) to process the tokens hidden state. Despite its advantages, the MoE inference system has to offload [4, 14, 44] the bloat of expert parameters to host memory and load them as needed for inference. This leads to massive synchronous stalls at every MoE layer. Recent works attempt to mitigate these GPU stalls through expert prefetching. Nevertheless, because MoE routing is highly dependent on the current tokens hidden states, existing methods are largely restricted to intra-token prediction. They leverage hidden states from earlier layers to predict later-layer routes for the current token. These approaches only yield microsecond-level computation window, which Specter is fundamentally insufficient to overlap with the millisecondlevel PCIe transfer latency of gigabyte-scale expert working sets. Extending to multi-step lookahead without verification mechanism is impractical; forcing the target model to execute based on unverified future predictions inevitably accumulates routing errors and degrades the final generation quality. Consequently, significant GPU stalls remain unresolved in current offloading systems.

sections.title: Lookahead
sections.content: Recently, speculative decoding [5, 25] offers principled solution to this dilemma by decoupling prediction from final execution. In SD, lightweight draft model rapidly generates sequence of 𝐾 future tokens, which the target model then verifies in parallel. This accept/reject mechanism mathematically guarantees lossless generation quality, even if the draft predictions are imperfect. For MoE offloading, the SD framework naturally provides multi-step time window to orchestrate PCIe prefetching. The drafting stage, running entirely in GPU VRAM, races ahead to generate future tokens. We can extract future expert routing information during this stage to orchestrate PCIe prefetching. Even if the draft model occasionally mispredicts, the verification stage guarantees that the final output distribution remains completely lossless. In traditional speculative decoding, smaller, independent model from the same family is typically employed as the draft. However, applying this paradigm to MoE offloading presents fundamental challenges. First, lack of routing correspondence: smaller dense model lacks an expert routing mechanism entirely, and even smaller MoE model possesses different routing space (e.g., different hidden dimensions or expert counts), making it impossible to directly map its expert activations to the target model. Second, poor universality and availability: not all open-source MoE families provide perfectly matched, lightweight counterpart, and training dedicated draft model incurs prohibitive costs. Third, memory redundancy: an independent draft model requires maintaining separate weights and redundant keyvalue (KV) cache, which severely exacerbates the memory wall and leaves less VRAM for caching experts. To overcome these hurdles and maximize the effectiveness of this speculative prefetching, the draft model must foresee the targets expert routing with high accuracy while minimizing additional memory overhead. Fortunately, we find that quantized version of the target MoE itself (e.g., INT4) serves as an ideal draft predictor. Because it shares the identical routing architecture and parameter lineage, it provides high-fidelity routing predictions without any training overhead. To demonstrate this, we measured the expert selection alignment between full-precision 16-bit floating-point (FP16) Qwen1.5-MoE (the target) and its INT4 quantized counterpart (the draft). For each token, we compared the top-4 experts selected by the draft against those selected by the target. Figure 2. All three distributions consistently peak above 90% with global mean of 90.8%, confirming that INT4 quantization preserves highfidelity expert routing across evaluated layers and inputs. Table 1 further confirms this trend across models, quantization methods, and precision settings. This high-fidelity, zero-training-cost predictability is transformative: it allows us to convert the highly non-deterministic, data-dependent expert routing problem into deterministic I/O prefetching and scheduling problem, enabling the orchestration of heavy PCIe transfers well in advance.

sections.title: 2.3 Speculative Offloading Needs System Efforts
sections.content: Naive integration introduces severe system-level bottlenecks. While quantized SD provides safe and high-fidelity lookahead mechanism, applying it directly to offloaded MoE inference introduces severe system-level challenge. VRAM contention limits expert caching. The fundamental challenge begins at the memory level. MoE offloading Wenfeng Wang et al. Figure 5. The high-level architecture of Specter. The system integrates Speculative Inference Controller, Predictive I/O Orchestrator, and Streamlined Execution Engine to transform I/O latency into productive computation through proactive data orchestration and adaptive control. draft model transforms already fine-grained MoE layers into tiny, fragmented INT4 kernels. Launching these fragmented kernels incurs disproportionately high overhead, leading to severe GPU underutilization during the critical draft phase. System-level co-design is imperative. Ultimately, these cascading bottlenecksfrom VRAM contention to I/O thrashing and fragmented executiondemonstrate that piecemeal optimization is insufficient. Translating the theoretical multistep lookahead of SD into actual end-to-end speedup in MoE offloading requires holistic co-design of model state management, I/O scheduling, and kernel execution. This fundamental requirement motivates the design of Specter.

sections.title:
3 Specter: System Architecture and Design
3.1 Design Principles and Architectural Overview
sections.content: Specter accelerates offloaded MoE inference by using multistep draft lookahead to overlap expert transfers with computation, while parallel target verification improves decoding efficiency. Three principles guide Specters design. First, transforming latency through speculation: lightweight quantized draft generates candidate tokens and expert-activation predictions during the I/O latency window, providing multi-step scheduling lookahead. Second, prediction-driven data orchestration: highfidelity routing predictions from 4-bit draft guide expert Figure 3. Increasing the speculative depth yields an approximately linear benefit in dense models, but markedly nonlinear trend in MoE models, as deeper speculation rapidly increases I/O demand under memory constraints. inherently targets memory-constrained environments, constraint that standard SD exacerbates by requiring the simultaneous maintenance of both draft and target model. Storing independent weights and maintaining redundant KV caches consumes precious GPU memory. Consequently, this redundancy leaves insufficient space for the crucial expert cache, directly degrading the systems baseline performance. Deep speculation triggers I/O thrashing. Beyond static capacity, speculative decoding introduces severe dynamic I/O pressure. In memory-constrained MoE inference, increasing the speculation depth 𝐾 triggers an expert explosion (Figure 3), as predicting 𝐾 tokens requires the union of experts activated across all steps. Figure 4 quantifies this effect across three MoE models. For example, on DeepSeekV2-Lite scaling 𝐾 from 1 to 16 expands the per-layer expert demand from 6.0 to 31.7, which is 5.3 surge covering nearly half of the total 64 experts. Once this enlarged working set exceeds the resident GPU cache, the required weights must be fetched synchronously over PCIe during target verification, causing heavy bus contention and critical-path I/O thrashing. Figure 4. Measured expert working-set growth with speculation depth. Fragmented execution causes pipeline bubbles. Even if the I/O bottleneck could be mitigated, the execution phase introduces its own inefficiencies. Traditional SD operates in strictly serial manner, which fails to deeply overlap draft computation, PCIe transfers, and target verification, resulting in massive pipeline stalls. Furthermore, quantizing the Specter prefetching, transfer timing, and verification order, using VRAM as an actively managed staging area for locality and reuse. Third, efficiency through tightly integrated execution: model state sharing, hybrid precision, fused kernels, and verification reordering jointly reduce draft, transfer, and verification overhead under tight memory budgets. As illustrated in Figure 5, Specter comprises three components: SIC coordinates hybrid-precision model sharing and decoding-state management; PIO converts multi-step lookahead into bandwidth-aware, three-phase PCIe prefetching; and SEE reduces execution fragmentation through kernel fusion, expert-wise reordering, and asynchronous overlap.

sections.title: 3.2 Speculative Inference Controller
sections.content: The Speculative Inference Controller serves as the control and organization layer of Specter. Rather than acting as heavyweight online optimizer, it is responsible for organizing the speculative workflow, managing the draft and target model instances, and maintaining speculation-related runtime state. In particular, it coordinates interactions between the draft and target models. This design reflects practical consideration in offloaded MoE inference: the benefit of speculation does not come only from accurate prediction, but also from whether the system can organize model state and speculative information in form that is directly usable by the expert scheduler and execution engine. The controller, therefore, provides stable control interface that bridges speculative decoding, expert scheduling, and system execution. The three SIC modules cover both the offline stage and online speculative inference: the Model Initializer constructs the shared drafttarget instance, the Speculative Depth Profiler selects 𝐾, and the Decoding State Manager runs each iteration and maintains committed token and KV states. Figure 6. Overview of parameter distribution and data layout orchestration in Specter.

sections.title: 3.3 Predictive I/O Orchestrator
sections.content: The PIO makes the experts required by target verification available in VRAM at the appropriate time, reducing stalls caused by on-demand PCIe transfers. As illustrated in Figure 9, PIO coordinates three modules across the draft and verification stages. During drafting, the Incremental Routing Pattern Analyzer aggregates expert activations into layerwise routing metadata, from which the Layer-Aware Prefetch Planner generates predictive host-to-device (H2D) transfers. Once target verification begins, the Verification Expert Cache Residency Manager uses the target routers authoritative routing decisions to coordinate compute queue for cachehit experts and an H2D queue for cache-miss experts, overlapping computation with the remaining H2D transfers. 3.3.1 Incremental Routing Pattern Analyzer. The Incremental Routing Pattern Analyzer records the expert IDs produced by the draft router, aggregates them into layer-wise routing metadata, and uses this metadata to guide subsequent expert prefetching. Conceptually, the ELB summarizes the top-𝑘 routing decisions generated across 𝐾 draft tokens and 𝐿 MoE layers. Specter implements it as GPU-resident, layer-indexed collection of activation counters. Only the counter representation is materialized and maintained on the GPU. At each prefetch checkpoint, the analyzer ranks experts in each layer by their cumulative activation counts and selects the top-𝑀 candidates, where 𝑀 matches the expert-cache capacity assigned to that layer. The selected layer-expert pairs are packed into compact prefetch plan and copied to the CPU runtime once per checkpoint. This checkpointlevel aggregation avoids frequent per-token transfers and reduces control-plane synchronization overhead. sections.title: 3.4 Streamlined Execution Engine
sections.content: The end-to-end performance of Specter ultimately depends on the efficiency of its execution engine. Once the speculative depth and expert prefetch plan have been determined, the execution engine is responsible for three tightly coupled Wenfeng Wang et al. Figure 11. Impact of quantization-aware fused expert kernels on throughput and latency in MoE models. Figure 12. Comparison of conventional token-wise verification and Specters cache-aware expert-wise execution. tasks: Draft Kernel Fusion accelerates proposal generation, Expert Verification Reordering restructures target-side MoE computation, and the Parallelism Optimizer coordinates computation and data movement to reduce pipeline stalls. In this way, the execution engine not only reduces kernel-level overhead, but also ensures that speculative prefetch can be effectively converted into practical end-to-end speedup. 3.4.1 Fine-Grained MoE Draft Kernel Fusion. We adopt GPTQ [15] for draft model quantization due to its favorable balance of implementation simplicity and accuracy retention. For execution backends, high-performance quantized engines such as Marlin [16] achieve superior throughput during prefill and standard dense decoding, as illustrated in Figure 10. However, Marlin is primarily optimized for large, regular general matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMMs) (e.g., evaluating up to 72K18K matrices). In contrast, modern finegrained MoE architectures employ much narrower expert matrices (such as 2,048 1,408 or 4,096 6,400), where each activated expert receives only small subset of the 𝐾 speculative tokens. In this regime, frequent kernel-launch overheads and poor Tensor Core utilization across fragmented expertlocal GEMMs counteract the benefits of low-bit arithmetic, occasionally rendering quantized execution slower than native FP16. To overcome this efficiency gap, Specter introduces fused multi-expert draft kernel. The kernel first gathers routed tokens by expert assignment and then schedules the disparate expert sub-computations into single fused GPU launch. This unified dispatch amortizes launch latency, maximizes thread-block occupancy, and consolidates sparse token activations into dense computational tiles. As shown in Figure 11, both the unfused and fused INT4 variants use the Marlin backend. This fusion improves draft decoding throughput on fine-grained MoE models with minimal overhead. 3.4.2 Cache-Aware Expert Verification Reordering. In conventional autoregressive decoding with batch size one, the target model processes exactly one token per step, enforcing strict chronological execution that precludes intertoken expert computation batching. Speculative decoding breaks this bottleneck by feeding candidate sequence of 𝐾 tokens into the target model in single forward pass. Specter leverages this verification lookahead window to fundamentally reorganize layer-wise MoE FFN computation. Figure 12 contrasts conventional token-wise verification with Specters cache-aware expert-wise execution. For each MoE layer, the target router first computes the authoritative routing decisions for all 𝐾 tokens. Rather than processing FFN of tokens in chronological order, Specter gathers tokens dispatched to identical experts and packs their activation states into contiguous sub-batches. This spatial aggregation converts fragmented, memory-bound general matrixvector multiplications (GEMVs) into dense, compute-bound GEMMs, maximizing the parallel compute capabilities of the GPU during target verification. Furthermore, Specter integrates this reordering with cache-aware execution schedule. It prioritizes the computation of cache-resident experts. Consider speculative window where tokens route to both resident expert and missing expert B. naive sequential approach would trigger immediate I/O stalls and potential cache thrashing. Conversely, Specter aggregates and immediately processes the sub-batch for expert A. Concurrently, it dispatches asynchronous H2D transfers for expert B. This schedule effectively hides the PCIe I/O latency behind the aggregated GEMM computation of resident experts. Upon completion of all expert sub-batches, Specter scatters the routing-weighted outputs. It accumulates them back into their original sequence positions. This transformation alters only the execution schedule of independent MoE FFN operations. It preserves the original target routing decisions. Attention mechanisms still evaluate using the standard causal mask. Finally, layer-wise synchronization ensures all tokens complete before advancing. Consequently, this expertwise reordering guarantees strict mathematical equivalence while substantially accelerating target verification.

4.1.3 Baselines. We evaluate Specter against six base-
lines spanning both mainstream serving frameworks and
research-oriented offloading designs. The first group con-
sists of three widely used inference frameworks: vLLM [24],
Transformers [55], and llama.cpp [17]. These baselines reflect
practical deployment stacks with different implementation
philosophies and provide a broad view of how Specter com-
pares against commonly used runtime systems. Concretely,
their default offloading behaviors differ substantially. vLLM
exposes CPU offloading as an on-demand weight offloading
mechanism. Transformers represents a more generic coarse-
grained offloading baseline, in which CPU-resident layers are
loaded on demand during execution. In contrast, llama.cpp
follows a CPU–GPU collaborative execution style, where
a configurable number of layers are offloaded to the GPU
while the remaining layers stay on the CPU, making it a
practical hybrid baseline for edge local deployment.

sections.content: The advantage is especially clear in the high-memory setting, where reduced memory pressure makes the execution efficiency of each system easier to expose. On Phi-3.5MoE, Specter achieves an average TPOT of 163.3 ms, compared with 292.1 ms for SpecMoEOff, 295.1 ms for MixtralOffloading-SM, 297.5 ms for vLLM, and 960.6 ms for Transformers, corresponding to up to 5.9 speedup over the generic Transformers baseline. On Qwen1.5-MoE, Specter reaches 35.3 ms/token, substantially outperforming SpecMoEOff (66.4 ms), Mixtral-Offloading-SM (74.2 ms), vLLM (176.6 ms), and Transformers (258.2 ms). Even on DeepSeekV2Lite, where the gap among stronger baselines is smaller, Specter still delivers the best overall performance, reducing average TPOT from 344.9 ms for Transformers to 72.2 ms. The same trend persists in the low-memory setting. Although tighter memory budgets amplify the cost of expert movement and narrow the gap between some baselines, Specter achieves the lowest TPOT on most datasets and in the per-model averages. In particular, it continues to outperform both speculative and non-speculative alternatives. This result suggests that the benefit of Specter does not depend on single favorable memory regime; rather, it continues to translate speculative lookahead into practical gains even when expert residency becomes more constrained. sections.title: 4.4 Impact of Prefetch Strategy
sections.content: We compare five cache-management policies in Figure 17. LRU is purely reactive: an expert is loaded only after being selected by the target router, and the least recently used expert in the same layer is evicted when necessary. LRU-S applies the same replacement policy with additional cache slots under the same total GPU-memory budget, isolating the benefit of increased cache capacity. SP-E and SP-L use the same ELB predictions and base cache capacity as Specter, but each prefetches once at its respective draft checkpoint. We conduct this study on DeepSeekV2-Lite under 16 GB, 24 GB, and 32 GB memory budgets. Cache hit rate is defined as the fraction of target-routed experts already available in GPU cache before on-demand loading, averaged across verification steps. Both single-prefetch policies substantially outperform reactive LRU, demonstrating the value of draftderived lookahead. By repeatedly refining the ELB and issuing incremental prefetch batches, Specter achieves the highest hit rate under every budget: 99.85%, 98.62%, and 96.25%, respectively. LRU-S becomes competitive at 32 GB because its larger cache retains more of the expert working set, but this improvement comes from additional cache capacity rather than predictive data movement.

sections.title:
5 Related Work
5.1 Efficient MoE Inference Systems
sections.content: MoE inference research [23, 30, 31, 51] addresses the memory and communication costs of large parameter footprints and data-dependent expert activation. General-purpose frameworks [2, 24, 55] support offloading, while specialized systems optimize expert placement and offloading [14, 42, 48, 59, 66, 67], caching, and prefetching [21, 45, 49, 65] using routing locality or predicted demand. Their overlap remains limited when demand is revealed only during target execution.

sections.title: 5.2 Speculative Decoding for LLMs
sections.content: Work on speculative decoding [5, 25] improves draft training [20, 53, 54, 61, 68], draft trees [13, 27, 50], verification [47, 56], runtime efficiency [6, 62], and dynamic speculation depth [3, 33], which balances draft overhead against acceptedtoken gains. For MoE, EARTH [29] and MoE-SpAc [26] use custom hardware or heterogeneous CPUGPU scheduling; SPMoE [7] requires structurally compatible drafttarget pairs without cross-model weight sharing; SpecMoEOff [52] emphasizes speculative I/O pipelining; and MoE-Spec [34] and SS-MoE [64] trade quality for efficiency through restricted or approximate expert execution. Specter couples speculative decoding with expert offloading, using quantized drafts multi-token routing lookahead for prefetching while standard target verification preserves the output distribution.

sections.title: 5.3 Quantization for LLM Inference
sections.content: Post-training and mixed-precision quantization reduce LLM memory and computation costs. SmoothQuant [57], AWQ [28], GPTQ [15] and other low-bit methods [9, 32, 37, 63] preserve model quality at reduced precision, while Marlin [16] accelerates inference through efficient low-bit GEMMs. Aggressive quantization can nevertheless degrade generation quality.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this paper, we presented Specter, speculative expertoffloading system for memory-constrained, single-GPU MoE inference. Using quantized draft model, Specter predicts expert routing across multiple future tokens and converts this lookahead into inter-token expert prefetching. It coordinates staged prefetching, verification-time expert residency, expert-wise execution, and fused draft computation to overlap PCIe transfers with computation. Evaluations demonstrate improved decoding latency and throughput across the evaluated models, workloads, memory budgets, and batch sizes. The system design of Specter allows speculative lookahead to improve execution performance without changing the target models output distribution.

Artifact Appendix A.1 Abstract Specter uses speculative expert offloading for MoE inference on single GPU with limited memory. This artifact provides installation instructions and scripts for decode latency, baseline comparisons, speculative depth, input length, and system measurements. The supplied DeepSeek-V2-Lite checkpoints support highand low-memory experiments with Specter, SpecMoEOff, and Mixtral-Offloading. Qwen1.5MoE and Phi-3.5-MoE are also supported with separately prepared checkpoints. The GitHub repository provides the source, checkpoint downloads, and complete instructions. A.2 Artifact check-list (meta-information) Algorithm: Speculative expert offloading for MoE inference. Run-time environment: Linux x86-64, Python 3.11.13, PyTorch 2.7.0 with CUDA runtime 12.6, and CUDA Toolkit 12.8. Hardware: One NVIDIA A100 GPU with 40 GB memory; the reference machine has 256 GB host memory. Disk space required: Approximately 200 GB for downloads, extracted checkpoints, the environment, and caches. Time needed to prepare workflow: About one hour, excluding downloads. Time needed to complete experiments: Approximately one hour for main, depth, and prefix; baseline Specter comparisons and other measurements require additional time. Publicly available?: Yes Archived DOI?: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22937478 A.3 Description A.3.1 How to access. The archived source corresponds to Git commit c0325dc. Download specter-ae-v1.tar. gz, specter-ae-wheels.tar.gz, specter-ae-datasets. tar.gz, SHA256SUMS, and specter-ae-v1.manifest.json from the Zenodo record. Choose workspace with sufficient free space and place these five files in its downloads/ directory: export SPECTER_WORK=/path/to/specter-work mkdir -p "$SPECTER_WORK/downloads" "$SPECTER_WORK/logs" Verify the files, extract the source, and download the prepared checkpoints from the DeepSeek release: cd "$SPECTER_WORK/downloads" sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS cd .. tar -xzf downloads/specter-ae-v1.tar.gz cd specter python3 -B initialization/download_models.py --manifest initialization/model-assets.json --output "$SPECTER_WORK/downloads" cd ../downloads sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS cd .. for in wheels datasets dsv2-target dsv2-draft do tar -xzf "downloads/specter-ae-$f.tar.gz" done unzip -n -P deserted-untie-orchid specter-assets/datasets/gpqa/gpqa_main.csv.zip -d specter-assets/datasets/gpqa/ Require four successful checks initially and six after downloading the models. Assets are extracted under specterassets/; the README provides complete download commands. A.3.2 Hardware dependencies. Experiments use one A100 40 GB GPU at batch size one. The reference platform has an Intel Xeon Silver 4310 CPU and 256 GB host memory for offloaded experts. NUMA binding is optional. A.3.3 Software dependencies. Requires CUDA driver, CUDA Toolkit 12.8, C++ compiler, Python 3.8 or newer for downloading, curl, tar, and unzip. The supplied wheels are GPTQModel 4.0.0.dev0, Transformers 4.53.3, FlashAttention 2.8.1, and vLLM 0.9.2. Use these validated builds; matching upstream version numbers are insufficient. The installer verifies wheel hashes and installs the remaining pinned dependencies from an online package index. A.3.4 Expected runtime. The reference main run takes about 20 minutes; each depth or prefix sweep takes about 20 30 minutes, including model loading. Baseline comparisons run three methods per memory setting. Runtime depends on the host and storage system. A.4 Installation Install uv without sudo and place caches and temporary build files on the work filesystem: cd "$SPECTER_WORK/specter" set -o pipefail curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/0.12.19/install.sh env UV_INSTALL_DIR="$HOME/.local/bin" sh export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" export UV_CACHE_DIR="$SPECTER_WORK/cache/uv" export UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR= "$SPECTER_WORK/cache/python" export TMPDIR="$SPECTER_WORK/cache/tmp" mkdir -p "$UV_CACHE_DIR" "$UV_PYTHON_INSTALL_DIR" "$TMPDIR" cp config.example.toml ../specter.local.toml export SPECTER_CONFIG= "$SPECTER_WORK/specter.local.toml" uv run --python 3.11.13 --no-project environment/install.py --config "$SPECTER_CONFIG" source "$SPECTER_WORK/env/bin/activate" The copied configuration matches the supplied assets. Relative paths resolve from its directory; edit them when reusing other assets. The environment, caches, and results remain outside the source tree. The installer pins flashinfer-python and applies environment/buildconstraints.txt, including torch==2.7.0, to its isolated build. Select an A100, set CUDA_HOME to the local CUDA 12.8 toolkit, validate resources, build kernels, and run the tests: export CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-12.8 export TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=8.0 MAX_JOBS=2 export PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 export PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 python -B -m configuration.check --config "$SPECTER_CONFIG" python -B -m streamlined_execution_engine.kernels.build python -B -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider tests baselines -q Continue after all checks succeed. The resource check validates checkpoint files and reads five nonempty inputs from each dataset. A.5 Alternate Setup: Existing Environment Update the source files to this release and reuse the installed environment, configuration, datasets, and DeepSeek checkpoints. Activate the environment, export SPECTER_CONFIG, and select the GPU and toolkit as above. The original main, depth, and prefix commands retain their workloads and parameters. A.6 Accessing DeepSeek-V2-Lite The public release supplies the target checkpoint, loaded in FP16, and draft with routed experts quantized to GPTQ INT4 (group size 128). No local quantization is needed. The download helper verifies and reconstructs the split archives and resumes interrupted downloads; GitHub login is not required. The five supplied datasets are GSM8K, WikiText-2, HumanEval, GPQA, and C4, with configuration keys GK, WT, HE, GP, and C4. A.7 Experiment workflow Keep SPECTER_CONFIG exported. Run the default highmemory main experiment and supporting sweeps: python -B -m benchmarks.run_ae python -B -m benchmarks.run_ae --experiment depth python -B -m benchmarks.run_ae --experiment prefix Use experiment all to run these three sequentially. The memory option accepts high, low, or both for main, all, and speedup. Run the low-memory main experiment or compare Specter with both baselines in both memory settings: python -B -m benchmarks.run_ae --experiment main --memory low --output ae_low mkdir -p "$SPECTER_WORK/logs" set -o pipefail python -B -m benchmarks.run_ae --experiment speedup --memory both --output ae_compare 2>&1 tee "$SPECTER_WORK/logs/ae_compare.log" The baseline implementations are in baselines/. High/low resident counts per layer are 16/4 for Specter, 12/2 for SpecMoEOff, and 32/20 for Mixtral-Offloading. Specter uses 𝐾 = 16; SpecMoEOff uses 𝐾 = 3. Routing and sensitivity measurements use: python -B -m benchmarks.run_ae --experiment routing python -B -m benchmarks.run_ae --experiment sensitivity Other experiment names are working-set, cache, ablation, latency, memory, fidelity, oracle, and kernel. Add dry-run to inspect commands before execution. Wenfeng Wang et al. A.8 Evaluation and expected results Results are saved under paths.output, which defaults to $SPECTER_WORK/results. The main run writes records. jsonl, summary.json, and summary.csv under ae/main/; the low-memory command above writes ae_low/main_ low/. The reference high-memory main run achieves approximately 70 ms/token. Depth profiling writes to ae/depth/ and selects the lowest-TPOT 𝐾. Prefix results are under ae/prefix_*/. The comparison command writes comparison.json and comparison.csv under ae_compare/speedup_high/ and ae_compare/speedup_low/, with per-method records below each. Tables report per-dataset and aggregate TPOT, speedup, output agreement, and GPU memory. Speedup is baseline mean decode TPOT divided by Specter mean decode TPOT. The external log records progress and results. Other measurements write ae/<experiment>/. Generate plots and source tables using the corresponding result directory: python -B -m benchmarks.plot_experiments --input "$SPECTER_WORK/results/ae/routing" Plots are saved in its figures/ subdirectory. A.9 Experiment customization Main and baseline comparisons use greedy decoding, five inputs from each of five datasets, three repeats, 16-token prefix cap, and 128 output tokens. Each method produces 75 records per memory setting. Depth and prefix sweeps use three GSM8K inputs, three repeats, and 128 output tokens. Depth tests 𝐾 {2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32}; prefix tests caps of 8, 16, and 32 tokens. See the README for custom workloads.
